L12-bcfb63: **Intradetrusor onabotulinumtoxinA (Botox)** is an FDA-approved, cystoscopically administered treatment for overactive bladder (OAB) at 100 U and neurogenic detrusor overactivity (NDO) at 200 U in patients inadequately managed by or intolerant of anticholinergic medications.<sup>[[1]](#ref1)[[2]](#ref2)</sup> It is also indicated for NDO in pediatric patients ≥ 5 years old, using a separate weight-based regimen.<sup>[[1]](#ref1)</sup> First reported for urological use by Schurch and colleagues in 2000, it has since become an established minimally invasive treatment for lower urinary tract dysfunction, with contemporary single-center data continuing to confirm the durability of response in real-world practice.<sup>[[3]](#ref3)[[10]](#ref10)</sup>
L14-f948c0: This page is the procedural counterpart to the [Botulinum Toxin pharmacology hub](/docs/foundations/pharmacology/storage-oab/botulinum-toxin), which holds the broader drug-class evidence (mechanism, off-label uses, head-to-head data, novel delivery systems). The 2024 AUA/SUFU OAB Guideline groups it with minimally invasive options alongside [Sacral Neuromodulation](/docs/surgical-techniques/04f-incontinence-procedures/procedures/sacral-neuromodulation) and [PTNS](/docs/surgical-techniques/04f-incontinence-procedures/procedures/percutaneous-tibial-nerve-stimulation).<sup>[[8]](#ref8)</sup>
L20-079e92: OnabotulinumtoxinA exerts a dual efferent and afferent mechanism in the bladder:<sup>[[4]](#ref4)[[5]](#ref5)[[6]](#ref6)</sup>
L22-7fa3a7: - **Efferent (motor) pathway.** Cleaves SNAP-25, a SNARE complex protein, thereby blocking acetylcholine release from peripheral cholinergic terminals, reducing detrusor contractile activity. It also blocks ATP release from purinergic efferent nerves.<sup>[[4]](#ref4)[[5]](#ref5)</sup>
L23-afd397: - **Afferent (sensory) pathway.** Reduces urothelial ATP release, decreases expression of capsaicin (TRPV1) and purinergic (P2X3) receptors on suburothelial sensory nerves, and reduces substance P and nerve growth factor levels. These observations support a sensory contribution to clinical benefit.<sup>[[5]](#ref5)[[6]](#ref6)</sup>
L24-dee580: - **Anti-inflammatory effects.** Decreases mast cell activation, reduces vascular endothelial growth factor expression, and attenuates neuroinflammation in the bladder wall.<sup>[[5]](#ref5)[[7]](#ref7)</sup>
L38-9be167: In the adult NDO pivotal program, 300 U offered no clinically relevant advantage over 200 U. In Ginsberg's trial, among those not catheterizing at baseline, CIC for retention began in 42% with 300 U, 35% with 200 U and 10% with placebo.<sup>[[11]](#ref11)[[12]](#ref12)[[13]](#ref13)</sup>
L46-d9c275: The two trials enrolled 275 (Cruz 2011) and 416 (Ginsberg 2012) participants. Both included SCI and MS; the pooled 310 SCI / 381 MS counts are diagnoses across trials, not separate trial populations:<sup>[[11]](#ref11)[[12]](#ref12)</sup>
L48-58e51a: - OnabotulinumtoxinA 200 U reduced UI episodes by 21.8/week versus 13.2/week for placebo at 6 weeks in Cruz's trial (p < 0.01).<sup>[[12]](#ref12)</sup>
L49-577781: - In a pooled meta-analysis of six RCTs (1,915 patients), 200 U increased maximum cystometric capacity (MCC) by 141 mL and decreased maximum detrusor pressure (MDP) by about 33 cm H₂O versus placebo (both p < 0.00001).<sup>[[13]](#ref13)</sup>
L50-bda2bd: - Median time to retreatment request: 256 days (200 U) versus 92 days (placebo).<sup>[[11]](#ref11)</sup>
L55-3c124e: Nitti's 557-patient RCT was one of the pivotal OAB trials (its 2017 publication is a reprint, not a separate trial):<sup>[[14]](#ref14)[[15]](#ref15)</sup>
L57-be802b: - OnabotulinumtoxinA 100 U reduced daily UI episodes by −2.65 versus −0.87 for placebo (p < 0.001).<sup>[[15]](#ref15)</sup>
L65-53d985: - Measure **post-void residual (PVR)**; caution if PVR > 100–200 mL.
L74-35cc34: - Performed via rigid or flexible cystoscope in the office or operating room according to patient, anesthesia and procedural needs.
L75-975e22: - Reconstitute onabotulinumtoxinA in 10 mL preservative-free normal saline for OAB 100 U or 30 mL for NDO 200 U.
L76-9cf4aa: - Use a cystoscopic injection needle appropriate for detrusor injection. The label specifies an insertion depth of about 2 mm into the detrusor, with injections spaced about 1 cm apart; needle length is not the intended depth.<sup>[[1]](#ref1)[[9]](#ref9)</sup>
L78-221062: - Inject into the detrusor muscle, distributing across the posterior and lateral bladder walls.
L79-e161de: - **Spare the trigone** (standard practice in the pivotal OAB trials, though some evidence suggests trigonal injection is safe). The AUA/SUFU guideline finds both trigone-sparing and trigone-including techniques effective; a small RCT favored sparing for incontinence at 6 months, with no difference in urgency, nocturia or OABSS.<sup>[[8]](#ref8)[[9]](#ref9)</sup>
L80-d5b2d4: - The labeled OAB template uses 20 sites. Reduced-site protocols are technique variations discussed in expert consensus; do not present 1–20 sites as one universally validated standard.<sup>[[17]](#ref17)</sup>
L81-a9e61e: - For adult NDO, 30 sites at 1 mL each is the labeled template; pediatric dosing differs as above.<sup>[[12]](#ref12)</sup>
L87-97a823: - Follow-up at 7–14 days to assess for urinary retention, which is highest about 2 weeks after injection.<sup>[[8]](#ref8)[[18]](#ref18)</sup>
L96-25852a: - Duration of effect: typically 4–10 months (median about 6–9 months for NDO; about 6 months for OAB).<sup>[[16]](#ref16)[[18]](#ref18)[[20]](#ref20)</sup>
L97-3c7e56: - Retreatment interval: no sooner than 12 weeks; expert consensus recommends scheduling at 6-month intervals with the option to retreat earlier if symptoms return.<sup>[[17]](#ref17)[[18]](#ref18)</sup>
L98-3c2bae: - Patients do not appear to become refractory to repeat injections over multiple cycles, though one retrospective study suggested possible declining duration after the 5th treatment cycle (from about 8.5–10.4 months to about 5.5 months).<sup>[[16]](#ref16)[[21]](#ref21)[[22]](#ref22)</sup>
L99-b87d51: - Across indications, the adult limit is 400 U per 3 months; pediatric total dose should not exceed the lower of 10 U/kg or 340 U per 3 months. Units are formulation-specific.<sup>[[1]](#ref1)</sup>
L118-049ceb: The adverse effect profile is primarily localized to the lower urinary tract:<sup>[[13]](#ref13)[[14]](#ref14)[[19]](#ref19)[[23]](#ref23)</sup>
L122-4ea384: - **Urinary tract infection.** In pooled OAB label trials, 18% versus 6% placebo within 12 weeks; definitions and follow-up differ across studies.<sup>[[1]](#ref1)</sup> For NDO, the cited meta-analysis reported RR 1.47 (95% CI 1.29–1.67) versus placebo.<sup>[[13]](#ref13)[[14]](#ref14)[[24]](#ref24)</sup>
L123-79f862: - **Urinary retention or CIC.** In pooled OAB trials, 6.5% initiated CIC versus 0.4% placebo over the treatment cycle (median catheterization 63 days). Retention was more frequent with diabetes (12.3% versus 6.3% without), as was UTI (31% versus 26%).<sup>[[1]](#ref1)</sup> Published retention rates range from 0% to 42.6% because definitions (PVR threshold, inability to void, CIC start) vary and are often omitted.<sup>[[40]](#ref40)</sup> NDO risk depends on baseline catheterization and dose; the non-catheterizing subgroup above gives one percentage that does not apply to all patients.<sup>[[3]](#ref3)[[11]](#ref11)[[12]](#ref12)[[13]](#ref13)[[14]](#ref14)</sup>

L134-d38610: In one retrospective cohort of 146 men with idiopathic OAB, 62.3% reported a treatment response and 13% had urinary retention. L140-fd56f6: The 2024 AUA/SUFU guideline supports selecting SNM, PTNS, or intradetrusor BTX through shared decision-making and permits minimally invasive therapy without requiring prior behavioral or medication trials (Expert Opinion). The FDA-labeled OAB indication still specifies inadequate response to or intolerance of an anticholinergic; distinguish guideline options from product labeling and coverage requirements.<sup>[[8]](#ref8)[[18]](#ref18)[[26]](#ref26)</sup>
L142-a8a8df: The EAU 2026 female LUTS guideline recommends onabotulinumtoxinA 100 U for OAB or UUI refractory to conservative or drug treatment (Strong). It advises warning patients about limited duration of response, UTI and possible prolonged intermittent catheterization (Strong), offering repeat injection when effective (Strong), and notes that other doses and other botulinum toxin A products are not licensed for OAB in Europe. It finds no difference between suburothelial and intradetrusor injection (level 1a), and higher voiding dysfunction and UTI rates than with antimuscarinics.<sup>[[41]](#ref41)</sup>
L144-736ebb: ROSETTA is a direct comparison with SNM. It randomized 386 women with refractory UUI; the published abstract describes 381 in its two assigned-treatment groups (192 Botox, 189 SNM), and 364 were available for primary analysis. These are different denominators, not separate trials. It used 200 U, above the labeled idiopathic OAB dose, so its benefit and harms cannot be transferred unchanged to 100-U treatment.<sup>[[38]](#ref38)</sup>
L152-a8834c: The primary between-group difference was 0.63 episode/day (95% CI 0.13–1.14): statistically significant, with uncertain clinical importance. The complete-resolution analysis required at least four monthly diaries and was exploratory. Greater symptom reduction came with more UTI and catheterization; it does not establish universal superiority. By 24 months the UUI reductions were similar (-3.88 versus -3.50 episodes/day, p=0.15), and recurrent UTI at 2 years remained higher with botulinum toxin (24% versus 10%), as reported in the AUA/SUFU guideline's review.<sup>[[8]](#ref8)[[38]](#ref38)</sup>
L154-1870aa: Systematic and network reviews combine different doses, populations, follow-up and outcome definitions; they should not be read as a definitive ranking of BTX, SNM and PTNS.<sup>[[27]](#ref27)[[28]](#ref28)</sup> Older real-world cost estimates are specific to their setting and year and do not give current patient prices.<sup>[[29]](#ref29)</sup>
L160-6bb603: MUSA (JAMA 2025) randomized 150 women with bothersome stress and urgency incontinence despite conservative or medical treatment; 137 contributed to the primary analysis. At six months, UDI total-score change was −66.8 with onabotulinumtoxinA 100 U versus −84.9 with midurethral sling (difference 18.1; 95% CI −4.6 to 40.7; p = 0.12). The sling produced greater improvement in the stress subscore (−45.2 versus −25.1), with similar irritative-subscore change. The trial did not demonstrate Botox superiority; it was not an equivalence trial. By 12 months, 22.6% had received both treatments. Discuss the likelihood of treating both symptom components and the different procedural risks.<sup>[[39]](#ref39)</sup>
L168-427f68: The AUA guideline lists intradetrusor onabotulinumtoxinA as a treatment option for [IC/BPS](/docs/clinical-conditions/03h-pelvic-pain/ic-pbs) when other treatments have failed, though evidence is Grade C.<sup>[[30]](#ref30)</sup> A meta-analysis of 12 RCTs demonstrated significant improvements in ICSI, ICPI, VAS pain scores, and daytime frequency, with small-to-medium effect sizes.<sup>[[31]](#ref31)</sup> Injection sites vary across studies (trigonal versus lateral or posterior walls), and the true effect is difficult to determine given the dearth of placebo-controlled trials of BTX alone.<sup>[[30]](#ref30)</sup>
L172-1d50d0: Injection of onabotulinumtoxinA into the external urethral sphincter (not intradetrusor) has been used for SCI patients with DSD, though this remains unlicensed.<sup>[[4]](#ref4)[[7]](#ref7)[[32]](#ref32)</sup>

L201-1e05d7: Two retrospective studies (about 1,170 injection episodes in total) found no clinically significant bleeding in patients on antithrombotic therapy. In a Danish cohort of 400 women with 1,059 treatments, zero cases of hematuria were reported despite 27.8% being on antithrombotics with no discontinuation.<sup>[[34]](#ref34)</sup> A second study of 114 injection episodes on full-dose anticoagulation or antiplatelet therapy reported only 0.88% spontaneously resolving hematuria.<sup>[[35]](#ref35)</sup> These observational cohorts support a low bleeding risk but do not establish that every antithrombotic should always continue, and the label advises stopping antiplatelets at least 3 days beforehand.<sup>[[1]](#ref1)</sup> Individualize the plan with the prescriber and procedural protocol.<sup>[[34]](#ref34)[[35]](#ref35)</sup>
L205-b0a771: A 29-year pharmacovigilance analysis identified 913 reported pregnancies across indications; the 0.7% major-defect estimate came from 1/152 prospectively reported live births, not all 913 reports. This observational denominator does not establish pregnancy safety. Most exposures (94.6%) occurred before conception or during the first trimester.<sup>[[36]](#ref36)</sup> Data remain limited, however, and onabotulinumtoxinA is not formally recommended during pregnancy.<sup>[[36]](#ref36)[[37]](#ref37)</sup>
L213-41b68b: - Patients should be counseled that the procedure is temporary and requires repeat treatments, and setting expectations early improves long-term adherence.<sup>[[17]](#ref17)</sup>
